narrative: A 25-year-old from Damascus fled when he faced conscription into the Syrian army as the civil war raged. He first went to Dubai, where he lived illegally for about two years, then moved on to Turkey and joined the flow of refugees and migrants heading toward Europe. The hardest part, he said, was the sea crossing from Turkey to Greece: a small inflatable rubber boat, overloaded, big waves, dangerous, with children and women crying. They tried twice. The first boat sank because it was too full, around 55 people, and they all swam back to the beach at sea. They tried again, and the second time succeeded; they reached Greece with no one hurt. From Greece he moved on to Hungary. At the Hungarian camp they were put outside in the rain and wind at night and were not allowed to leave. So everyone in the camp agreed together to go on strike, and only then did the authorities agree to open the gate and let them go on to Budapest. At the Budapest train station ordinary people were kind, giving food, water and clothes, but when he tried to board a train the police cut him back. So the group planned to board one train together so the police could not stop them, and they all bought tickets on one train to the border. From the border to Austria they walked. In Austria people were waiting for them, asking if anyone needed a doctor, handing out blankets and jackets, and providing buses to take them to the train station to continue the journey. The first city he reached in Germany was Munich. He was surprised when he entered the train station to find a crowd of people waiting, with food, drink, everything, even phone cards. He spoke from a camp north of Berlin. Asked whether he would go back to Syria, he said it depends: if the war ended there he would return, because it is his hometown and his father, mother and little brother are still there.
